title: SMTP Service Extension for Authentication
summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets a client name an authentication mechanism, run an authentication exchange with the server, and optionally set up a security layer for the rest of the session. It works by profiling the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) for SMTP. It replaces RFC 2554.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4954 adds an SMTP AUTH command that lets a client authenticate with a mechanism chosen from the server's advertised SASL list. It can also negotiate a security layer and let the client attach an authenticated submission identity to an individual message.

subtitle: Adds SASL authentication and sender-identity information to SMTP sessions.

tldr.problem: SMTP needs a standard way for a client to authenticate to a server and optionally protect the rest of the session.
tldr.mechanism: The AUTH command runs a selected SASL exchange, and an AUTH parameter on MAIL FROM can identify the mailbox associated with a message's submission.
tldr.outcome: SMTP servers can authenticate submitters and carry submission identity between trusted servers. RFC 4954 obsoletes RFC 2554 and is updated by RFC 5248.

today: RFC 4954 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2554 and updates RFC 3463. It is updated by RFC 5248.

sections.title: Authentication for SMTP
sections.content:
The Authentication service extension lets an SMTP client choose a Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) mechanism and exchange messages with the server to authenticate. A successful exchange may also establish a security layer for later SMTP commands.

The server advertises the AUTH extension and the mechanisms it supports in its response to EHLO. The mechanism list may change after STARTTLS, so clients must use the capabilities reported after the TLS negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: SMTP AUTH lets a client prove its identity to an email server using a selected authentication method. The server advertises which methods it accepts.

sections.title: The AUTH Command Exchange
sections.content:
The client starts authentication with AUTH and a mechanism name, optionally including an initial response. The server sends challenges and the client replies with Base64-encoded SASL data until authentication succeeds or fails.

The client can cancel an exchange, and a successful command cannot be repeated within the same SMTP session. If a security layer is negotiated, SMTP returns to its initial protocol state and the client should issue EHLO again.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server exchange challenge and response messages until the mechanism accepts or rejects the login. If authentication also turns on a security layer, both sides refresh their SMTP capabilities.

sections.title: The AUTH Parameter on MAIL FROM
sections.content:
The optional AUTH parameter on MAIL FROM identifies the mailbox associated with the identity that submitted the message. A value of AUTH=<> means that the original submitter is unknown or not sufficiently authenticated.

Trusted servers can pass this information when relaying a message to another server that supports the extension. The parameter describes submission identity; it does not prove who authored the message's content.
sections.plainLanguage: The MAIL FROM command can carry the identity associated with a message's submission. This helps trusted servers preserve that information while relaying mail, but it does not authenticate the message's author.

sections.title: Authentication Results and Requirements
sections.content:
SMTP response codes distinguish successful authentication, invalid credentials, temporary failures, and mechanisms that are too weak for server policy. A server can also require authentication before allowing other SMTP commands.

To support interoperability, implementations must support SASL PLAIN over TLS. A server must have a configuration that prevents password mechanisms vulnerable to eavesdropping from being used without an external security layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Response codes tell a client whether login worked, failed temporarily, or needs a different method. Password-based methods must be protected by TLS or another security layer.

sections.title: What SMTP AUTH Protects
sections.content:
SMTP AUTH authenticates message submission and can protect the message envelope when a security layer is used. It is not a replacement for end-to-end message signing or encryption and does not establish authorship of the message body.

Before SASL begins, SMTP interactions are sent in the clear and may be changed by an active attacker. Clients that depend on a secure server connection should require mutual authentication and encryption rather than silently continuing after authentication failures.
sections.plainLanguage: SMTP AUTH can verify who submitted a message and protect the connection when combined with suitable security. It does not prove who wrote the message or replace end-to-end email security.
